From Contact to Creole: How New Languages Are Born

A  When people who share no common language need to communicate regularly, for example in trade or on plantations, they often develop a simplified form of speech that draws on elements of the languages around them. Linguists call such a system a pidgin. Pidgins typically have a small vocabulary, much of it taken from the language of the most powerful group, and a reduced grammar in which features such as verb endings and grammatical gender are absent. Crucially, a pidgin is nobody's first language: its speakers use it only for limited purposes and continue to speak their own languages at home.

B  The story becomes more interesting when children grow up in a community where a pidgin is the main shared language. In such circumstances, the pidgin may become the first language of a new generation, and when this happens it typically expands dramatically. Its vocabulary grows to cover every area of life, and it acquires consistent grammatical structures for expressing time, possibility and complex relationships between ideas. A language that has developed in this way is known as a creole. Haitian Creole, for example, which draws much of its vocabulary from French, is now the first language of almost the entire population of Haiti and has had official status alongside French since 1987.

C  The transition need not be sudden. Tok Pisin, spoken in Papua New Guinea, began as a pidgin used among workers from many different language groups in the nineteenth century. Over time it spread as a common language in a country where several hundred languages are spoken, and it is now the first language of a growing number of people, particularly in towns. Tok Pisin is used in parliament, in newspapers and on the radio, and is one of the country's official languages. Its development illustrates how the boundary between pidgin and creole can be gradual rather than clear-cut.

D  Creoles have attracted attention from linguists far beyond their own regions because they appear to offer a natural experiment in how languages are created. The American linguist Derek Bickerton, who studied the English-based creole of Hawaii, argued that the children of plantation workers there had created a complete language within a single generation. Because creoles in different parts of the world share certain grammatical features despite having different source languages, he proposed that these features reflect an innate human capacity for language. This hypothesis has been strongly contested. Critics point out that the shared features might be explained by the languages that the original speakers brought with them, and that the historical evidence about how quickly creoles formed is often incomplete.

E  A remarkable case from Central America has added a new dimension to the debate. In the late 1970s and 1980s, schools for deaf children were established in Nicaragua, bringing together children who had previously had little contact with one another and who used only simple home-made gestures. Within a few years, the children had developed a shared sign language. Researchers observed that children who joined at a younger age used the language more fluently and with more systematic grammar than older members of the community, suggesting that young learners played a central role in its development.

F  Despite their scientific interest, creoles have often been regarded with contempt, dismissed as 'broken' versions of European languages. Speakers have frequently been discouraged from using them in schools, sometimes being punished for doing so. Linguists today reject the idea that creoles are inferior; they are complete languages capable of expressing anything their speakers need to say. Increasingly, educators argue that children whose first language is a creole learn more effectively when they are first taught to read in that language, and some education systems have begun to put this idea into practice.

A  In 1729, the French astronomer Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Mairan conducted a simple experiment. He had observed that the leaves of a mimosa plant opened during the day and folded at night, and he wondered whether the plant was simply responding to sunlight. To find out, he placed it in a dark cupboard. To his surprise, the leaves continued to open and close at roughly the usual times, even though the plant could not detect the sun. De Mairan did not pursue the matter further, but his observation is now recognised as the first evidence of an internal biological clock.

B  It is now known that almost all living things, from bacteria to humans, possess such clocks. They generate rhythms in physiology and behaviour, known as circadian rhythms from the Latin words meaning 'about a day'. The word 'about' is important: when people are isolated from all external time cues, for example in caves or windowless laboratories, their daily cycle of sleeping and waking continues but typically runs slightly longer than twenty-four hours. Under normal conditions, the clock is reset each day by environmental signals, the most powerful of which is light.

C  The molecular basis of the clock was uncovered largely through research on fruit flies. In the early 1970s, researchers identified flies with mutations in a single gene that disrupted their daily rhythms: some had cycles that were too short, others too long, and others had no rhythm at all. The gene was named 'period'. In the 1980s, three American scientists, Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young, isolated this gene and later showed how it worked. The protein it produces builds up in cells during the night and then blocks the activity of its own gene, so that levels fall again during the day. This self-regulating loop, which takes about twenty-four hours to complete, forms the core of the clock. The three researchers were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2017.

D  In mammals, a master clock is located in a small region of the brain called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which receives information about light directly from the eyes. Interestingly, the cells mainly responsible for detecting light for this purpose are not the rods and cones used for vision, but a separate group of cells in the retina that are especially sensitive to blue light. The master clock coordinates subsidiary clocks found in almost every organ, including the liver, heart and kidneys, ensuring that processes such as digestion, hormone release and body temperature follow a consistent daily pattern.

E  Modern life frequently brings these clocks into conflict with the environment. Travellers crossing several time zones experience jet lag because their internal clock takes several days to adjust to local time; most people find adjusting after flying east harder than after flying west, because it is generally easier to delay the clock than to advance it. Night-shift workers face a more persistent problem, since they must remain awake when their bodies are prepared for sleep. Long-term shift work has been associated with higher rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease, and the World Health Organization's cancer research agency has classified night-shift work as probably carcinogenic.

F  Research on circadian rhythms is also beginning to influence medicine. Because the activity of many enzymes and receptors varies through the day, the effectiveness and side effects of some drugs depend on when they are taken, and clinicians are investigating whether timing treatments more carefully could improve outcomes. There is also growing interest in how individual differences in clock timing, known as chronotypes, affect health and performance. Teenagers, for example, tend to have later chronotypes than adults, which has prompted some schools to experiment with later start times.

Fresh Water from the Sea

A  Around 97 per cent of the Earth's water is found in the oceans, too salty to drink or to use for most agriculture. It is hardly surprising, then, that turning seawater into fresh water has long been regarded as an ideal solution to water shortages. Sailors were boiling seawater and collecting the steam centuries ago, and today desalination is a major industry: thousands of plants operate worldwide, concentrated particularly in the Middle East and North Africa, where some countries depend on them for most of their drinking water. Yet I believe the technology is too often presented either as a miracle or as a disaster, when the truth lies somewhere in between.

B  Early large-scale plants relied on heat. In a process called multi-stage flash distillation, seawater is heated and passed through a series of chambers kept at progressively lower pressures, causing part of it to boil instantly, or 'flash', into steam, which is then condensed as fresh water. Thermal methods are reliable but consume large amounts of energy, which is why they were adopted mainly in countries with abundant oil and gas. Since the 1980s, they have increasingly been overtaken by reverse osmosis, a technique in which seawater is forced at high pressure through membranes that allow water molecules to pass but block salt.

C  Reverse osmosis has become far more efficient over the past few decades. Improved membranes and devices that recover energy from the high-pressure waste stream have reduced the electricity needed to produce a cubic metre of fresh water to a fraction of what it once was. Even so, desalination remains more energy-intensive than most conventional water sources, and if that energy comes from fossil fuels, it adds to greenhouse gas emissions. In my view, linking new plants to renewable energy should be a condition of their approval rather than an optional extra.

D  The second major concern is brine, the concentrated salt solution left over after fresh water has been extracted. A widely cited study published in 2019 estimated that, globally, desalination plants produce more brine than fresh water. Most of it is returned to the sea, where, because it is denser than seawater, it can sink and spread across the seabed, potentially harming marine organisms. Careful design of outflow pipes can help the brine to mix more rapidly, and researchers are investigating ways of extracting useful minerals from it, but such approaches are not yet widely applied.

E  Israel offers an instructive example of what desalination can achieve. After a series of droughts in the early 2000s, the country built several large reverse-osmosis plants along its Mediterranean coast, which now supply a large proportion of its household water. Combined with extensive recycling of wastewater for agriculture, this has transformed a country once facing severe shortages into one with a relatively secure supply. Critics, however, note that such investment requires substantial financial resources and technical capacity, which many water-scarce countries lack.

F  For these reasons, I would argue that desalination should generally be considered only after cheaper and less damaging options. Repairing leaking pipes, which in some cities lose a third or more of treated water, and recycling wastewater are often more cost-effective. Nevertheless, for coastal cities facing growing populations and declining rainfall, desalination can provide a supply that does not depend on the weather, and that reliability has considerable value. The challenge is to ensure that it is used wisely rather than as a substitute for good water management.

It is hardly surprising, then, that turning seawater into fresh water has long been regarded as an ideal solution to water shortages. Sailors were boiling seawater and collecting the steam centuries ago, and today desalination is a major industry: thousands of plants operate worldwide, concentrated particularly in the Middle East and North Africa, where some countries depend on them for most of their drinking water. Yet I believe the technology is too often presented either as a miracle or as a disaster, when the truth lies somewhere in between.

B  Early large-scale plants relied on heat. In a process called multi-stage flash distillation, seawater is heated and passed through a series of chambers kept at progressively lower pressures, causing part of it to boil instantly, or 'flash', into steam, which is then condensed as fresh water. Thermal methods are reliable but consume large amounts of energy, which is why they were adopted mainly in countries with abundant oil and gas. Since the 1980s, they have increasingly been overtaken by reverse osmosis, a technique in which seawater is forced at high pressure through membranes that allow water molecules to pass but block salt.

C  Reverse osmosis has become far more efficient over the past few decades. Improved membranes and devices that recover energy from the high-pressure waste stream have reduced the electricity needed to produce a cubic metre of fresh water to a fraction of what it once was. Even so, desalination remains more energy-intensive than most conventional water sources, and if that energy comes from fossil fuels, it adds to greenhouse gas emissions. In my view, linking new plants to renewable energy should be a condition of their approval rather than an optional extra.

D  The second major concern is brine, the concentrated salt solution left over after fresh water has been extracted. A widely cited study published in 2019 estimated that, globally, desalination plants produce more brine than fresh water. Most of it is returned to the sea, where, because it is denser than seawater, it can sink and spread across the seabed, potentially harming marine organisms. Careful design of outflow pipes can help the brine to mix more rapidly, and researchers are investigating ways of extracting useful minerals from it, but such approaches are not yet widely applied.

E  Israel offers an instructive example of what desalination can achieve. After a series of droughts in the early 2000s, the country built several large reverse-osmosis plants along its Mediterranean coast, which now supply a large proportion of its household water. Combined with extensive recycling of wastewater for agriculture, this has transformed a country once facing severe shortages into one with a relatively secure supply. Critics, however, note that such investment requires substantial financial resources and technical capacity, which many water-scarce countries lack.

F  For these reasons, I would argue that desalination should generally be considered only after cheaper and less damaging options. Repairing leaking pipes, which in some cities lose a third or more of treated water, and recycling wastewater are often more cost-effective. Nevertheless, for coastal cities facing growing populations and declining rainfall, desalination can provide a supply that does not depend on the weather, and that reliability has considerable value. The challenge is to ensure that it is used wisely rather than as a substitute for good water management.
